analysis.one_liner: Gives seniors a more accurate cost-of-living adjustment and applies Social Security taxes to all earnings, not just the first $128,400.
analysis.headline: Introduced with five Democratic senators in 2017, the bill never received a hearing, markup, or vote in the Senate Finance Committee and died when the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have made two changes to Social Security. First, it would have calculated the program's annual cost-of-living adjustment using a price index built around what people 62 and older actually buy — mainly health care and housing — instead of the index for younger urban workers. Second, it would have gradually removed the earnings cap below which wages are taxed for Social Security (about $128,400 in 2018), so that all earnings would eventually be subject to the 12.4% payroll tax, while counting a portion of those higher earners' extra contributions toward modestly larger benefits for them.
analysis.who_benefits: Current and future Social Security beneficiaries — retirees, people with disabilities, and survivors — would get cost-of-living adjustments that better track their own expenses, which tend to rise faster than the index used now. Low-income beneficiaries would gain the most, and the bill explicitly protects anyone receiving SSI or Medicaid from losing benefits because of the larger checks. Over time, applying the payroll tax to all earnings would also improve the program's finances.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Current and future Social Security beneficiaries

how_it_helps.text: Directs the Bureau of Labor Statistics to publish a Consumer Price Index for Elderly Consumers (CPI-E) tracking costs typical of people 62 and older, and requires Social Security to use it for annual cost-of-living adjustments instead of the index for urban wage earners.

Phases in the removal of the taxable earnings cap over 2018-2023 (86% of wages above the cap taxed in 2018, declining to 0% excluded after 2023), so all wages and self-employment income would eventually be subject to Social Security tax.
Counts a portion of earnings above the old cap in the benefit formula at low rates (3% and 0.25% tiers), so high earners who pay tax on all their income receive some additional benefit in return.

Specifies that any benefit increase from the new inflation index does not count as income or resources when determining eligibility for Supplemental Security Income or Medicaid, so low-income beneficiaries would not lose other assistance.

analysis.who_pays: High earners — people with wages or self-employment income above the roughly $128,400 cap — would pay the 12.4% Social Security tax (including the full self-employment rate) on all of their earnings after the phase-in. High earners would recover some of this through the new benefit tiers, but at a much lower rate than what they pay in.
analysis.who_pays_short: High earners above the payroll cap

drawbacks.text: The phase-out of the cap is a large, permanent tax increase on high earners: 12.4 cents of every dollar above the old cap, with self-employed people paying both the employee and employer shares out of their own income.

Switching to the CPI-E would increase benefit growth above what current law provides, adding to the program's costs; the bill covers part of this with the new tax revenue but the new benefit tiers for high earners offset some of that revenue.
The bill had no Republican support and was never examined in committee, so its interactions with the program's long-term financing were never publicly tested in a hearing.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For the roughly 60 million-plus Americans who receive Social Security, the changes are straightforwardly favorable: a more accurate inflation measure and no benefit cuts. The cost falls narrowly on high earners, who would pay tax on income that is currently exempt. The honest trade-off is that the bill shifts a substantial tax burden onto the top slice of earners without any bipartisan vetting of its financing assumptions — which is exactly why it never moved.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Senate Finance Committee on the day it was introduced and sat there for the rest of the Congress — no hearing, no markup, no floor vote — before expiring in January 2019.

narrative.text: Senator Hirono introduced the bill on July 20, 2017, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Finance the same day.
No further action was ever recorded: the Finance Committee held no hearing or markup on the bill, and it never reached the Senate floor.
Four Democratic senators cosponsored the bill; no Republican did.
The bill expired when the 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019, with all introduced bills not passed.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: High earners who would have paid Social Security tax on all of their wages and self-employment income are better off, since the bill died without any of its provisions taking effect. So is anyone who preferred that any change to Social Security financing go through a bipartisan process; the bill's backers gained nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: High earners above the payroll cap

for.name: Sen. Mazie Hirono
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and served as its lead sponsor.

for.name: Sen. Jeff Merkley
for.what_they_did: Joined as the bill's original cosponsor at introduction.

against.name: Sen. Orrin Hatch
against.what_they_did: Took no recorded action on the bill after it was referred to the Finance Committee — no hearing, markup, or vote was ever scheduled.

sides.party_line_note: All five Senate supporters were Democrats — the sponsor and four cosponsors — and no Republican signed on, while the Republican-run Finance Committee gave the bill no action.

industries.note: The bill would have ended the roughly $128,400 exemption, subjecting all wages and self-employment income to the 12.4% Social Security tax after a six-year phase-in. Self-employed people would bear the full tax on their own income, though the bill grants them modestly higher benefits in return.
